title: Resolutions
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 70 personal resolutions for holy living, written between ages 18 and 20.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 1
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 1. Resolved, that I will do whatsoever I think to be most to God's glory, and my own good, profit and pleasure, in the whole of my duration, without any consideration of the time, whether now, or never so many myriad's of ages hence. Resolved to do whatever I think to be my duty …

title: Resolutions — Resolution 2
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 2. Resolved, to be continually endeavoring to find out some new invention and contrivance to promote the aforementioned things.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 3
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 3. Resolved, if ever I shall fall and grow dull, so as to neglect to keep any part of these Resolutions, to repent of all I can remember, when I come to myself again.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 4
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 4. Resolved, never to do any manner of thing, whether in soul or body, less or more, but what tends to the glory of God; nor be, nor suffer it, if I can avoid it.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 5
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 5. Resolved, never to lose one moment of time; but improve it the most profitable way I possibly can.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 6
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 6. Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 7
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 7. Resolved, never to do anything, which I should be afraid to do, if it were the last hour of my life.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 8
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 8. Resolved, to act, in all respects, both speaking and doing, as if nobody had been so vile as I, and as if I had committed the same sins, or had the same infirmities or failings as others; and that I will let the knowledge of their failings promote nothing but shame in myself, …

title: Resolutions — Resolution 9
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 9. Resolved, to think much on all occasions of my own dying, and of the common circumstances which attend death.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 10
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 10. Resolved, when I feel pain, to think of the pains of martyrdom, and of hell.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 11
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 11. Resolved, when I think of any theorem in divinity to be solved, immediately to do what I can towards solving it, if circumstances don't hinder.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 12
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 12. Resolved, if I take delight in it as a gratification of pride, or vanity, or on any such account, immediately to throw it by.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 13
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 13. Resolved, to be endeavoring to find out fit objects of charity and liberality.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 14
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 14. Resolved, never to do anything out of revenge.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 15
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 15. Resolved, never to suffer the least motions of anger to irrational beings.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 16
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 16. Resolved, never to speak evil of anyone, so that it shall tend to his dishonor, more or less, upon no account except for some real good.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 17
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 17. Resolved, that I will live so as I shall wish I had done when I come to die.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 18
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 18. Resolved, to live so at all times, as I think is best in my devout frames, and when I have clearest notions of things of the gospel, and another world.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 19
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 19. Resolved, never to do anything, which I should be afraid to do, if I expected it would not be above an hour, before I should hear the last trump.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 20
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 20. Resolved, to maintain the strictest temperance in eating and drinking.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 21
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 21. Resolved, never to do anything, which if I should see in another, I should count a just occasion to despise him for, or to think any way the more meanly of him.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 22
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 22. Resolved, to endeavor to obtain for myself as much happiness, in the other world, as I possibly can, with all the power; might, vigor, and vehemence, yea violence, I am capable of, or can bring myself to exert, in any way that can be thought of.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 23
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 23. Resolved, frequently to take some deliberate action, which seems most unlikely to be done, for the glory of God, and trace it back to the original intention, designs and ends of it; and if I find it not to be for God's glory, to repute it as a breach of the 4th Resolution.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 24
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 24. Resolved, whenever I do any conspicuously evil action, to trace it back, till I come to the original cause; and then both carefully endeavor to do so no more, and to fight and pray with all my might against the original of it.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 25
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 25. Resolved, to examine carefully, and constantly, what that one thing in me is, which causes me in the least to doubt of the love of God; and to direct all my forces against it.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 26
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 26. Resolved, to cast away such things, as I find do abate my assurance.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 27
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 27. Resolved, never willfully to omit anything, except the omission be for the glory of God; and frequently to examine my omissions.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 28
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 28. Resolved, to study the Scriptures so steadily, constantly and frequently, as that I may find, and plainly perceive myself to grow in the knowledge of the same.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 29
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 29. Resolved, never to count that a prayer, nor to let that pass as a prayer, nor that as a petition of a prayer, which is so made, that I cannot hope that God will answer it; nor that as a confession, which I cannot hope God will accept.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 30
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 30. Resolved, to strive to my utmost every week to be brought higher in religion, and to a higher exercise of grace, than I was the week before.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 31
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 31. Resolved, never to say anything at all against anybody, but when it is perfectly agreeable to the highest degree of Christian honor, and of love to mankind, agreeable to the lowest humility, and sense of my own faults and failings, and agreeable to the golden rule; often, whe…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 32
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 32. Resolved, to be strictly and firmly faithful to my trust, that that in Prov. 20:6, "A faithful man who can find?" may not be partly fulfilled in me.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 33
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 33. Resolved, always to do what I can towards making, maintaining, establishing and preserving peace, when it can be without over-balancing detriment in other respects. Dec.26, 1722.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 34
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 34. Resolved, in narration's never to speak anything but the pure and simple verity.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 35
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 35. Resolved, whenever I so much question whether I have done my duty, as that my quiet and calm is thereby disturbed, to set it down, and also how the question was resolved. Dec. 18, 1722.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 36
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 36. Resolved, never to speak evil of any, except I have some particular good call for it. Dec. 19, 1722.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 37
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 37. Resolved, to inquire every night, as I am going to bed, wherein I have been negligent, what sin I have committed, and wherein I have denied myself: also at the end of every week, month and year. Dec.22 and 26, 1722.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 38
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 38. Resolved, never to speak anything that is ridiculous, sportive, or matter of laughter on the Lord's day. Sabbath evening, Dec. 23, 1722.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 39
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 39. Resolved, never to do anything that I so much question the lawfulness of, as that I intend, at the same time, to consider and examine afterwards, whether it be lawful or no; except I as much question the lawfulness of the omission.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 40
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 40. Resolved, to inquire every night, before I go to bed, whether I have acted in the best way I possibly could, with respect to eating and drinking. Jan. 7, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 41
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 41. Resolved, to ask myself at the end of every day, week, month and year, wherein I could possibly in any respect have done better. Jan. 11, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 42
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 42. Resolved, frequently to renew the dedication of myself to God, which was made at my baptism; which I solemnly renewed, when I was received into the communion of the church; and which I have solemnly re-made this twelfth day of January, 1722-23.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 43
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 43. Resolved, never henceforward, till I die, to act as if I were any way my own, but entirely and altogether God's, agreeable to what is to be found in Saturday, January 12. Jan.12, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 44
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 44. Resolved, that no other end but religion, shall have any influence at all on any of my actions; and that no action shall be, in the least circumstance, any otherwise than the religious end will carry it. Jan.12, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 45
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 45. Resolved, never to allow any pleasure or grief, joy or sorrow, nor any affection at all, nor any degree of affection, nor any circumstance relating to it, but what helps religion. Jan.12 and 13.1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 46
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 46. Resolved, never to allow the least measure of any fretting uneasiness at my father or mother. Resolved to suffer no effects of it, so much as in the least alteration of speech, or motion of my eve: and to be especially careful of it, with respect to any of our family.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 47
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 47. Resolved, to endeavor to my utmost to deny whatever is not most agreeable to a good, and universally sweet and benevolent, quiet, peace able, contented, easy, compassionate, generous, humble, meek, modest, submissive, obliging, diligent and industrious, charitable, even, pati…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 48
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 48. Resolved, constantly, with the utmost niceness and diligence, and the strictest scrutiny, to be looking into the state of my soul, that I may know whether I have truly an interest in Christ or no; that when I come to die, I may not have any negligence respecting this to repen…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 49
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 49. Resolved, that this never shall be, if I can help it.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 50
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 50. Resolved, I will act so as I think I shall judge would have been best, and most prudent, when I come into the future world. July 5, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 51
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 51. Resolved, that I will act so, in every respect, as I think I shall wish I had done, if I should at last be damned. July 8, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 52
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 52. I frequently hear persons in old age say how they would live, if they were to live their lives over again: Resolved, that I will live just so as I can think I shall wish I had done, supposing I live to old age. July 8, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 53
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 53. Resolved, to improve every opportunity, when I am in the best and happiest frame of mind, to cast and venture my soul on the Lord Jesus Christ, to trust and confide in him, and consecrate myself wholly to him; that from this I may have assurance of my safety, knowing that I c…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 54
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 54. Whenever I hear anything spoken in conversation of any person, if I think it would be praiseworthy in me, Resolved to endeavor to imitate it. July 8, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 55
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 55. Resolved, to endeavor to my utmost to act as I can think I should do, if I had already seen the happiness of heaven, and hell torments. July 8, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 56
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 56. Resolved, never to give over, nor in the least to slacken my fight with my corruptions, however unsuccessful I may be.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 57
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 57. Resolved, when I fear misfortunes and adversities, to examine whether ~ have done my duty, and resolve to do it; and let it be just as providence orders it, I will as far as I can, be concerned about nothing but my duty and my sin. June 9, and July 13 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 58
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 58. Resolved, not only to refrain from an air of dislike, fretfulness, and anger in conversation, but to exhibit an air of love, cheerfulness and benignity. May27, and July 13, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 59
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 59. Resolved, when I am most conscious of provocations to ill nature and anger, that I will strive most to feel and act good-naturedly; yea, at such times, to manifest good nature, though I think that in other respects it would be disadvantageous, and so as would be imprudent at …

title: Resolutions — Resolution 60
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 60. Resolved, whenever my feelings begin to appear in the least out of order, when I am conscious of the least uneasiness within, or the least irregularity without, I will then subject myself to the strictest examination. July 4, and 13, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 61
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 61. Resolved, that I will not give way to that listlessness which I find unbends and relaxes my mind from being fully and fixedly set on religion, whatever excuse I may have for it-that what my listlessness inclines me to do, is best to be done, etc. May 21, and July 13, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 62
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 62. Resolved, never to do anything but duty; and then according to Eph. 6:6-8, do it willingly and cheerfully as unto the Lord, and not to man; "knowing that whatever good thing any man doth, the same shall he receive of the Lord." June 25 and July 13, 1723.

author: Jonathan Edwards

author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 64. Resolved, when I find those "groanings which cannot be uttered" (Rom. 8:26), of which the Apostle speaks, and those "breakings of soul for the longing it hath," of which the Psalmist speaks, Psalm 119:20, that I will promote them to the utmost of my power, and that I will not…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 65
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 65. Resolved, very much to exercise myself in this all my life long, viz. with the greatest openness I am capable of, to declare my ways to God, and lay open my soul to him: all my sins, temptations, difficulties, sorrows, fears, hopes, desires, and every thing, and every circums…

title: Resolutions — Resolution 66
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 66. Resolved, that I will endeavor always to keep a benign aspect, and air of acting and speaking in all places, and in all companies, except it should so happen that duty requires otherwise.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 67
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 67. Resolved, after afflictions, to inquire, what I am the better for them, what good I have got by them, and what I might have got by them.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 68
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 68. Resolved, to confess frankly to myself all that which I find in myself, either infirmity or sin; and, if it be what concerns religion, also to confess the whole case to God, and implore needed help. July 23, and August 10, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 69
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 69. Resolved, always to do that, which I shall wish I had done when I see others do it. Aug. 11, 1723.

title: Resolutions — Resolution 70
author: Jonathan Edwards
snippet: 70. Let there be something of benevolence, in all that I speak. Aug. 17, 1723

title: The Heidelberg Catechism
snippet: 129 questions and answers for the Christian life, organized into 52 Lord's Days.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 1, Q. 1
snippet: What is your only comfort in life and death?
body: That I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. He has fully paid for all my sins with his precious blood, and has set me free from all the power of the devil. He also preserves me in such a way that without the…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 1, Q. 2
snippet: What do you need to know in order to live and die in the joy of this comfort?
body: First, how great my sins and misery are; second, how I am delivered from all my sins and misery; third, how I am to be thankful to God for such deliverance.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 2, Q. 3
snippet: From where do you know your sins and misery?
body: From the law of God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 2, Q. 4
snippet: What does God's law require of us?
body: Christ teaches us this in a summary in Matthew 22: Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: Love your neighbour as yourself. All the Law and the Prophets hang o…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 2, Q. 5
snippet: Can you keep all this perfectly?
body: No, I am inclined by nature to hate God and my neighbour.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 3, Q. 6
snippet: Did God, then, create man so wicked and perverse?
body: No, on the contrary, God created man good and in his image, that is, in true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God his Creator, heartily love him, and live with him in eternal blessedness to praise and glorify him.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 3, Q. 7
snippet: From where, then, did man's depraved nature come?
body: From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise, for there our nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 3, Q. 8
snippet: But are we so corrupt that we are totally unable to do any good and inclined to all evil?
body: Yes, unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 4, Q. 9
snippet: But does not God do man an injustice by requiring in his law what man cannot do?
body: No, for God so created man that he was able to do it. But man, at the instigation of the devil, in deliberate disobedience robbed himself and all his descendants of these gifts.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 4, Q. 10
snippet: Will God allow such disobedience and apostasy to go unpunished?
body: Certainly not. He is terribly displeased with our original sin as well as our actual sins. Therefore he will punish them by a just judgment both now and eternally, as he has declared: Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law (Gal 3:…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 4, Q. 11
snippet: But is God not also merciful?
body: God is indeed merciful, but he is also just. His justice requires that sin committed against the most high majesty of God also be punished with the most severe, that is, with everlasting, punishment of body and soul.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 5, Q. 12
snippet: Since, according to God's righteous judgment we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, how can we escape this punishment and be again received into favour?
body: God demands that his justice be satisfied. Therefore we must make full payment, either by ourselves or through another.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 5, Q. 13
snippet: Can we by ourselves make this payment?
body: Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 5, Q. 14
snippet: Can any mere creature pay for us?
body: No. In the first place, God will not punish another creature for the sin which man has committed. Furthermore, no mere creature can sustain the burden of God's eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 5, Q. 15
snippet: What kind of mediator and deliverer must we seek?
body: One who is a true and righteous man, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is at the same time true God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 6, Q. 16
snippet: Why must he be a true and righteous man?
body: He must be a true man because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should pay for sin. He must be a righteous man because one who himself is a sinner cannot pay for others.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 6, Q. 17
snippet: Why must he at the same time be true God?
body: He must be true God so that by the power of his divine nature he might bear in his human nature the burden of God's wrath, and might obtain for us and restore to us righteousness and life.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 6, Q. 18
snippet: But who is that Mediator who at the same time is true God and a true and righteous man?
body: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who has become for us wisdom from God — that is, our righteousness, holiness and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 6, Q. 19
snippet: From where do you know this?
body: From the holy gospel, which God himself first revealed in Paradise. Later, he had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law. Finally, he had it fulfilled through his only Son.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 7, Q. 20
snippet: Are all men, then, saved by Christ just as they perished through Adam?
body: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all his benefits.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 7, Q. 21
snippet: What is true faith?
body: True faith is a sure knowledge whereby I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in his Word. At the same time it is a firm confidence that not only to others, but also to me, God has granted forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation, out of mere grace,…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 7, Q. 22
snippet: What, then, must a Christian believe?
body: All that is promised us in the gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in a summary.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 7, Q. 23
snippet: What are these articles?
body: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth. I believe in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord; he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary; suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried; he descended into hell. On …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 8, Q. 24
snippet: How are these articles divided?
body: Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 8, Q. 25
snippet: Since there is only one God, why do you speak of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
body: Because God has so revealed himself in his Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 9, Q. 26
snippet: What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth?
body: That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and who still upholds and governs them by his eternal counsel and providence, is, for the sake of Christ his Son, my God and my Father. In him I trust so complet…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 10, Q. 27
snippet: What do you understand by the providence of God?
body: God's providence is his almighty and ever present power, whereby, as with his hand, he still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so governs them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 10, Q. 28
snippet: What does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by his providence?
body: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we can have a firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from his love; for all creatures are so completely in his hand that without his will they cannot s…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 11, Q. 29
snippet: Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour?
body: Because he saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 11, Q. 30
snippet: Do those who seek their salvation or well-being in saints, in themselves, or anywhere else, also believe in the only Saviour Jesus?
body: No. Though they boast of him in words, they in fact deny the only Saviour Jesus. For one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith accept this Saviour must find in him all that is necessary for their salvation.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 12, Q. 31
snippet: Why is he called Christ, that is, Anointed?
body: Because he has been ordained by God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of his body has redeem…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 12, Q. 32
snippet: Why are you called a Christian?
body: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and thus share in his anointing, so that I may as prophet confess his name, as priest present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to him, and as king fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and h…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 13, Q. 33
snippet: Why is he called God's only-begotten Son, since we also are children of God?
body: Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 13, Q. 34
snippet: Why do you call him our Lord?
body: Because he has ransomed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with his precious blood, and has freed us from all the power of the devil to make us his own possession.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 14, Q. 35
snippet: What do you confess when you say: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary?
body: The eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary, through the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus he is also the true seed of David, and like his brothers in every respect, yet without si…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 14, Q. 36
snippet: What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ?
body: He is our Mediator, and with his innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin, in which I was conceived and born.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 15, Q. 37
snippet: What do you confess when you say that he suffered?
body: During all the time he lived on earth, but especially at the end, Christ bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Thus, by his suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, he has redeemed our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtain…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 15, Q. 38
snippet: Why did he suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge?
body: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, and so he freed us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 15, Q. 39
snippet: Does it have a special meaning that Christ was crucified and did not die in a different way?
body: Yes. Thereby I am assured that he took upon himself the curse which lay on me, for a crucified one was cursed by God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 16, Q. 40
snippet: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble himself even unto death?
body: Because of the justice and truth of God satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 16, Q. 41
snippet: Why was he buried?
body: His burial testified that he had really died.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 16, Q. 42
snippet: Since Christ has died for us, why do we still have to die?
body: Our death is not a payment for our sins, but it puts an end to sin and is an entrance into eternal life.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 16, Q. 43
snippet: What further benefit do we receive from Christ's sacrifice and death on the cross?
body: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified, put to death, and buried with him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 16, Q. 44
snippet: Why is there added: He descended into hell?
body: In my greatest sorrows and temptations I may be assured and comforted that my Lord Jesus Christ, by his unspeakable anguish, pain, terror, and agony, which he endured throughout all his sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 17, Q. 45
snippet: How does Christ's resurrection benefit us?
body: First, by his resurrection he has overcome death, so that he could make us share in the righteousness which he had obtained for us by his death. Second, by his power we too are raised up to a new life. Third, Christ's resurrection is to us a sure pledge of our glorious resurrecti…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 18, Q. 46
snippet: What do you confess when you say, he ascended into heaven?
body: That Christ, before the eyes of his disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that he is there for our benefit until he comes again to judge the living and the dead.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 18, Q. 47
snippet: Is Christ, then, not with us until the end of the world, as he has promised us?
body: Christ is true man and true God. With respect to his human nature he is no longer on earth, but with respect to his divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit he is never absent from us.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 18, Q. 48
snippet: But are the two natures in Christ not separated from each other if his human nature is not present wherever his divinity is?
body: Not at all, for his divinity has no limits and is present everywhere. So it must follow that his divinity is indeed beyond the human nature which he has taken on and nevertheless is within this human nature and remains personally united with it.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 18, Q. 49
snippet: How does Christ's ascension into heaven benefit us?
body: First, he is our Advocate in heaven before his Father. Second, we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that he, our Head, will also take us, his members, up to himself. Third, he sends us his Spirit as a counter-pledge, by whose power we seek the things that are above, where…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 19, Q. 50
snippet: Why is it added, and sits at the right hand of God?
body: Christ ascended into heaven to manifest himself there as Head of his church, through whom the Father governs all things.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 19, Q. 51
snippet: How does the glory of Christ, our Head, benefit us?
body: First, by his Holy Spirit he pours out heavenly gifts upon us, his members. Second, by his power he defends and preserves us against all enemies.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 19, Q. 52
snippet: What comfort is it to you that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead?
body: In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and eagerly await as judge from heaven the very same person who before has submitted himself to the judgment of God for my sake, and has removed all the curse from me. He will cast all his and my enemies into everlasting condemna…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 20, Q. 53
snippet: What do you believe concerning the Holy Spirit?
body: First, he is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, he is also given to me, to make me by true faith share in Christ and all his benefits, to comfort me, and to remain with me forever.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 21, Q. 54
snippet: What do you believe concerning the holy catholic Christian church?
body: I believe that the Son of God, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, defends, and preserves for himself, by his Spirit and Word, in the unity of the true faith, a church chosen to everlasting life. And I believe that I am and forever sh…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 21, Q. 55
snippet: What do you understand by the communion of saints?
body: First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with him and share in all his treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is duty-bound to use his gifts readily and cheerfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 21, Q. 56
snippet: What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins?
body: I believe that God, because of Christ's satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, nor my sinful nature, against which I have to struggle all my life, but will graciously grant me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never come into condemnation.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 22, Q. 57
snippet: What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you?
body: Not only shall my soul after this life immediately be taken up to Christ, my Head, but also this my flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made like Christ's glorious body.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 22, Q. 58
snippet: What comfort do you receive from the article about the life everlasting?
body: Since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived — a blessedness in which to praise God forever.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 23, Q. 59
snippet: But what does it help you now that you believe all this?
body: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 23, Q. 60
snippet: How are you righteous before God?
body: Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments, have never kept any of them, and am still inclined to all evil, yet God, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, imputes to me the perfect s…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 23, Q. 61
snippet: Why do you say that you are righteous only by faith?
body: Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God. I can receive this righteousness and make it my own by faith only.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 24, Q. 62
snippet: But why can our good works not be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it?
body: Because the righteousness which can stand before God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 24, Q. 63
snippet: But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the next?
body: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 24, Q. 64
snippet: Does this teaching not make people careless and wicked?
body: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 25, Q. 65
snippet: Since then faith alone makes us share in Christ and all his benefits, where does this faith come from?
body: From the Holy Spirit, who works it in our hearts by the preaching of the gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the sacraments.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 25, Q. 66
snippet: What are the sacraments?
body: The sacraments are holy, visible signs and seals. They were instituted by God so that by their use he might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the gospel. And this is the promise: that God graciously grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life because of …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 25, Q. 67
snippet: Are both the Word and the sacraments then intended to focus our faith on the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation?
body: Yes, indeed. The Holy Spirit teaches us in the gospel and assures us by the sacraments that our entire salvation rests on Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 25, Q. 68
snippet: How many sacraments has Christ instituted in the new covenant?
body: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 26, Q. 69
snippet: How does holy baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you?
body: In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing and with it gave the promise that, as surely as water washes away the dirt from the body, so certainly his blood and Spirit wash away the impurity of my soul, that is, all my sins.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 26, Q. 70
snippet: What does it mean to be washed with Christ's blood and Spirit?
body: To be washed with Christ's blood means to receive forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, because of Christ's blood, poured out for us in his sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with his Spirit means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified to be members of Christ, s…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 26, Q. 71
snippet: Where has Christ promised that he will wash us with his blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism?
body: In the institution of baptism, where he says: Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Mt 28:19). Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 27, Q. 72
snippet: Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?
body: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 27, Q. 73
snippet: Why then does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins?
body: God speaks in this way for a good reason. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ remove our sins just as water takes away dirt from the body. But, even more important, he wants to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly cleansed from our si…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 27, Q. 74
snippet: Should infants, too, be baptized?
body: Yes. Infants as well as adults belong to God's covenant and congregation. Through Christ's blood the redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who works faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Therefore, by baptism, as sign of the covenant, they must be incorporated in…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 28, Q. 75
snippet: How does the Lord's supper signify and seal to you that you share in Christ's one sacrifice on the cross and in all his gifts?
body: In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup in remembrance of him. With this command he gave these promises: First, as surely as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup given to me, so surely …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 28, Q. 76
snippet: What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink his shed blood?
body: First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and so receive forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, to be united more and more to his sacred body through the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. Therefore, although Christ is…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 28, Q. 77
snippet: Where has Christ promised that he will nourish and refresh believers with his body and blood as surely as they eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup?
body: In the institution of the Lord's supper: The Lord Jesus, on the night he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, "This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me." In the same way, after supper he took the cup, saying, "This c…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 29, Q. 78
snippet: Are then the bread and wine changed into the real body and blood of Christ?
body: No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ and is not the washing away of sins itself but is simply God's sign and pledge, so also the bread in the Lord's supper does not become the body of Christ itself, although it is called Christ's body in keepin…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 29, Q. 79
snippet: Why then does Christ call the bread his body and the cup his blood, or the new covenant in his blood, and why does Paul speak of a participation in the body and blood of Christ?
body: Christ speaks in this way for a good reason: He wants to teach us by his supper that as bread and wine sustain us in this temporal life, so his crucified body and shed blood are true food and drink for our souls to eternal life. But, even more important, he wants to assure us by …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 30, Q. 80
snippet: What difference is there between the Lord's supper and the papal mass?
body: The Lord's supper testifies to us, first, that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which he himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and, second, that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with his true …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 30, Q. 81
snippet: Who are to come to the table of the Lord?
body: Those who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 30, Q. 82
snippet: Are those also to be admitted to the Lord's supper who by their confession and life show that they are unbelieving and ungodly?
body: No, for then the covenant of God would be profaned and his wrath kindled against the whole congregation. Therefore, according to the command of Christ and his apostles, the Christian church is duty-bound to exclude such persons by the keys of the kingdom of heaven, until they ame…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 31, Q. 83
snippet: What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven?
body: The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 31, Q. 84
snippet: How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the gospel?
body: According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened when it is proclaimed and publicly testified to each and every believer that God has really forgiven all their sins for the sake of Christ's merits, as often as they by true faith accept the promise of the gospel…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 31, Q. 85
snippet: How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by church discipline?
body: According to the command of Christ, people who call themselves Christians but show themselves to be unchristian in doctrine or life are first repeatedly admonished in a brotherly manner. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 32, Q. 86
snippet: Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we yet do good works?
body: Because Christ, having redeemed us by his blood, also renews us by his Holy Spirit to be his image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for his benefits, and he may be praised by us. Further, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruit…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 32, Q. 87
snippet: Can those be saved who do not turn to God from their ungrateful and impenitent walk of life?
body: By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or the like shall inherit the kingdom of God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 33, Q. 88
snippet: What is the true repentance or conversion of man?
body: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 33, Q. 89
snippet: What is the dying of the old nature?
body: It is to grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we have offended God by our sin, and more and more to hate it and flee from it.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 33, Q. 90
snippet: What is the coming to life of the new nature?
body: It is a heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and a love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 33, Q. 91
snippet: But what are good works?
body: Only those which are done out of true faith, in accordance with the law of God, and to his glory, and not those based on our own opinion or on precepts of men.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 34, Q. 92
snippet: What is the law of the LORD?
body: God spoke all these words: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. 1. You shall have no other gods before me. 2. You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters belo…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 34, Q. 93
snippet: How are these commandments divided?
body: Into two parts. The first teaches us how to live in relation to God; the second, what duties we owe our neighbour.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 34, Q. 94
snippet: What does the LORD require in the first commandment?
body: That for the sake of my very salvation I avoid and flee all idolatry, witchcraft, superstition, and prayer to saints or to other creatures. Further, that I rightly come to know the only true God, trust in him alone, submit to him with all humility and patience, expect all good fr…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 34, Q. 95
snippet: What is idolatry?
body: Idolatry is having or inventing something in which to put our trust instead of, or in addition to, the only true God who has revealed himself in his Word.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 35, Q. 96
snippet: What does God require in the second commandment?
body: We are not to make an image of God in any way, nor to worship him in any other manner than he has commanded in his Word.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 35, Q. 97
snippet: May we then not make any image at all?
body: God cannot and may not be visibly portrayed in any way. Creatures may be portrayed, but God forbids us to make or have any images of them in order to worship them or to serve God through them.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 35, Q. 98
snippet: But may images not be tolerated in the churches as "books for the laity"?
body: No, for we should not be wiser than God. He wants his people to be taught not by means of dumb images but by the living preaching of his Word.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 36, Q. 99
snippet: What is required in the third commandment?
body: We are not to blaspheme or to abuse the name of God by cursing, perjury, or unnecessary oaths, nor to share in such horrible sins by being silent bystanders. Rather, we must use the holy name of God only with fear and reverence, so that we may rightly confess him, call upon him, …

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 36, Q. 100
snippet: Is the blaspheming of God's name by swearing and cursing such a grievous sin that God is angry also with those who do not prevent and forbid it as much as they can?
body: Certainly, for no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more than the blaspheming of his name. That is why he commanded it to be punished with death.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 37, Q. 101
snippet: But may we swear an oath by the name of God in a godly manner?
body: Yes, when the government demands it of its subjects, or when necessity requires it, in order to maintain and promote fidelity and truth, to God's glory and for our neighbour's good. Such oath-taking is based on God's Word and was therefore rightly used by saints in the Old and th…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 37, Q. 102
snippet: May we also swear by saints or other creatures?
body: No. A lawful oath is a calling upon God, who alone knows the heart, to bear witness to the truth, and to punish me if I swear falsely. No creature is worthy of such honour.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 38, Q. 103
snippet: What does God require in the fourth commandment?
body: First, that the ministry of the gospel and the schools be maintained and that, especially on the day of rest, I diligently attend the church of God to hear God's Word, to use the sacraments, to call publicly upon the LORD, and to give Christian offerings for the poor. Second, tha…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 39, Q. 104
snippet: What does God require in the fifth commandment?
body: That I show all honour, love, and faithfulness to my father and mother and to all those in authority over me, submit myself with due obedience to their good instruction and discipline, and also have patience with their weaknesses and shortcomings, since it is God's will to govern…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 40, Q. 105
snippet: What does God require in the sixth commandment?
body: I am not to dishonour, hate, injure, or kill my neighbour by thoughts, words, or gestures, and much less by deeds, whether personally or through another; rather, I am to put away all desire of revenge. Moreover, I am not to harm or recklessly endanger myself. Therefore, also, the…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 40, Q. 106
snippet: But does this commandment speak only of killing?
body: By forbidding murder God teaches us that he hates the root of murder, such as envy, hatred, anger, and desire of revenge, and that he regards all these as murder.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 40, Q. 107
snippet: Is it enough, then, that we do not kill our neighbour in any such way?
body: No. When God condemns envy, hatred, and anger, he commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, to show patience, peace, gentleness, mercy, and friendliness toward him, to protect him from harm as much as we can, and to do good even to our enemies.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 41, Q. 108
snippet: What does the seventh commandment teach us?
body: That all unchastity is cursed by God. We must therefore detest it from the heart and live chaste and disciplined lives, both within and outside of holy marriage.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 41, Q. 109
snippet: Does God in this commandment forbid nothing more than adultery and similar shameful sins?
body: Since we, body and soul, are temples of the Holy Spirit, it is God's will that we keep ourselves pure and holy. Therefore he forbids all unchaste acts, gestures, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever may entice us to unchastity.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 42, Q. 110
snippet: What does God forbid in the eighth commandment?
body: God forbids not only outright theft and robbery but also such wicked schemes and devices as false weights and measures, deceptive merchandising, counterfeit money, and usury; we must not defraud our neighbour in any way, whether by force or by show of right. In addition God forbi…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 42, Q. 111
snippet: What does God require of you in this commandment?
body: I must promote my neighbour's good wherever I can and may, deal with him as I would like others to deal with me, and work faithfully so that I may be able to give to those in need.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 43, Q. 112
snippet: What is required in the ninth commandment?
body: I must not give false testimony against anyone, twist no one's words, not gossip or slander, nor condemn or join in condemning anyone rashly and unheard. Rather, I must avoid all lying and deceit as the devil's own works, under penalty of God's heavy wrath. In court and everywher…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 44, Q. 113
snippet: What does the tenth commandment require of us?
body: That not even the slightest thought or desire contrary to any of God's commandments should ever arise in our heart. Rather, with all our heart we should always hate all sin and delight in all righteousness.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 44, Q. 114
snippet: But can those converted to God keep these commandments perfectly?
body: No. In this life even the holiest have only a small beginning of this obedience. Nevertheless, with earnest purpose they do begin to live not only according to some but to all the commandments of God.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 44, Q. 115
snippet: If in this life no one can keep the ten commandments perfectly, why does God have them preached so strictly?
body: First, so that throughout our life we may more and more become aware of our sinful nature, and therefore seek more eagerly the forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ. Second, so that, while praying to God for the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may never stop striving to be…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 45, Q. 116
snippet: Why is prayer necessary for Christians?
body: Because prayer is the most important part of the thankfulness which God requires of us. Moreover, God will give his grace and the Holy Spirit only to those who constantly and with heartfelt longing ask him for these gifts and thank him for them.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 45, Q. 117
snippet: What belongs to a prayer which pleases God and is heard by him?
body: First, we must from the heart call upon the one true God only, who has revealed himself in his Word, for all that he has commanded us to pray. Second, we must thoroughly know our need and misery, so that we may humble ourselves before God. Third, we must rest on this firm foundat…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 45, Q. 118
snippet: What has God commanded us to ask of him?
body: All the things we need for body and soul, as included in the prayer which Christ our Lord himself taught us.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 46, Q. 120
snippet: Why has Christ commanded us to address God as our Father?
body: To awaken in us at the very beginning of our prayer that childlike reverence and trust toward God which should be basic to our prayer: God has become our Father through Christ and will much less deny us what we ask of him in faith than our fathers would refuse us earthly things.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 46, Q. 121
snippet: Why is there added, in heaven?
body: These words teach us not to think of God's heavenly majesty in an earthly manner, and to expect from his almighty power all things we need for body and soul.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 49, Q. 124

body: Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. That is: Grant that we and all men may deny our own will, and without any murmuring obey your will, for it alone is good. Grant also that everyone may carry out the duties of his office and calling as willingly and faithfully as the…

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 52, Q. 128
snippet: How do you conclude your prayer?
body: For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. That is: All this we ask of you because, as our King, having power over all things, you are both willing and able to give us all that is good, and because not we but your holy name should so receive all glory forever.

title: The Heidelberg Catechism — Lord's Day 52, Q. 129
snippet: What does the word Amen mean?
body: Amen means: It is true and certain. For God has much more certainly heard my prayer than I feel in my heart that I desire this of him.

title: The 95 Theses
author: Martin Luther
snippet: 95 propositions challenging the sale of indulgences, sparking the Protestant Reformation.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 1
author: Martin Luther
snippet: When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, “Repent” (Mt 4:17), he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 2
author: Martin Luther
snippet: This word cannot be understood as referring to the sacrament of penance, that is, confession and satisfaction, as administered by the clergy.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 3
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Yet it does not mean solely inner repentance; such inner repentance is worthless unless it produces various outward mortification of the flesh.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 4
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The penalty of sin remains as long as the hatred of self (that is, true inner repentance), namely till our entrance into the kingdom of heaven.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 5
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The pope neither desires nor is able to remit any penalties except those imposed by his own authority or that of the canons.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 6
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The pope cannot remit any guilt, except by declaring and showing that it has been remitted by God; or, to be sure, by remitting guilt in cases reserved to his judgment. If his right to grant remission in these cases were disregarded, the guilt would certainly remain unforgiven.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 7
author: Martin Luther
snippet: God remits guilt to no one unless at the same time he humbles him in all things and makes him submissive to the vicar, the priest.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 8
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The penitential canons are imposed only on the living, and, according to the canons themselves, nothing should be imposed on the dying.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 9
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Therefore the Holy Spirit through the pope is kind to us insofar as the pope in his decrees always makes exception of the article of death and of necessity.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 10
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Those priests act ignorantly and wickedly who, in the case of the dying, reserve canonical penalties for purgatory.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 11
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Those tares of changing the canonical penalty to the penalty of purgatory were evidently sown while the bishops slept (Mt 13:25).

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 12
author: Martin Luther
snippet: In former times canonical penalties were imposed, not after, but before absolution, as tests of true contrition.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 13
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The dying are freed by death from all penalties, are already dead as far as the canon laws are concerned, and have a right to be released from them.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 14
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Imperfect piety or love on the part of the dying person necessarily brings with it great fear; and the smaller the love, the greater the fear.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 15
author: Martin Luther
snippet: This fear or horror is sufficient in itself, to say nothing of other things, to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near to the horror of despair.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 16
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Hell, purgatory, and heaven seem to differ the same as despair, fear, and assurance of salvation.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 17
author: Martin Luther
snippet: It seems as though for the souls in purgatory fear should necessarily decrease and love increase.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 18
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Furthermore, it does not seem proved, either by reason or by Scripture, that souls in purgatory are outside the state of merit, that is, unable to grow in love.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 19
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Nor does it seem proved that souls in purgatory, at least not all of them, are certain and assured of their own salvation, even if we ourselves may be entirely certain of it.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 20
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Therefore the pope, when he uses the words “plenary remission of all penalties,” does not actually mean “all penalties,” but only those imposed by himself.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 21
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Thus those indulgence preachers are in error who say that a man is absolved from every penalty and saved by papal indulgences.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 22
author: Martin Luther
snippet: As a matter of fact, the pope remits to souls in purgatory no penalty which, according to canon law, they should have paid in this life.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 23
author: Martin Luther
snippet: If remission of all penalties whatsoever could be granted to anyone at all, certainly it would be granted only to the most perfect, that is, to very few.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 24
author: Martin Luther
snippet: For this reason most people are necessarily deceived by that indiscriminate and high-sounding promise of release from penalty.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 25
author: Martin Luther
snippet: That power which the pope has in general over purgatory corresponds to the power which any bishop or curate has in a particular way in his own diocese and parish.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 26
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The pope does very well when he grants remission to souls in purgatory, not by the power of the keys, which he does not have, but by way of intercession for them.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 27
author: Martin Luther
snippet: They preach only human doctrines who say that as soon as the money clinks into the money chest, the soul flies out of purgatory.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 28
author: Martin Luther
snippet: It is certain that when money clinks in the money chest, greed and avarice can be increased; but when the church intercedes, the result is in the hands of God alone.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 29
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Who knows whether all souls in purgatory wish to be redeemed, since we have exceptions in St. Severinus and St. Paschal, as related in a legend.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 30
author: Martin Luther
snippet: No one is sure of the integrity of his own contrition, much less of having received plenary remission.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 31
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The man who actually buys indulgences is as rare as he who is really penitent; indeed, he is exceedingly rare.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 32
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Those who believe that they can be certain of their salvation because they have indulgence letters will be eternally damned, together with their teachers.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 33
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Men must especially be on guard against those who say that the pope’s pardons are that inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 34
author: Martin Luther
snippet: For the graces of indulgences are concerned only with the penalties of sacramental satisfaction established by man.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 35
author: Martin Luther
snippet: They who teach that contrition is not necessary on the part of those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessional privileges preach unchristian doctrine.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 36
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Any truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without indulgence letters.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 37
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Any true Christian, whether living or dead, participates in all the blessings of Christ and the church; and this is granted him by God, even without indulgence letters.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 38
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Nevertheless, papal remission and blessing are by no means to be disregarded, for they are, as I have said (Thesis 6), the proclamation of the divine remission.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 39
author: Martin Luther
snippet: It is very difficult, even for the most learned theologians, at one and the same time to commend to the people the bounty of indulgences and the need of true contrition.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 40
author: Martin Luther
snippet: A Christian who is truly contrite seeks and loves to pay penalties for his sins; the bounty of indulgences, however, relaxes penalties and causes men to hate them — at least it furnishes occasion for hating them.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 41
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Papal indulgences must be preached with caution, lest people erroneously think that they are preferable to other good works of love.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 42
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that the pope does not intend that the buying of indulgences should in any way be compared with works of mercy.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 43
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that he who gives to the poor or lends to the needy does a better deed than he who buys indulgences.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 44
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Because love grows by works of love, man thereby becomes better. Man does not, however, become better by means of indulgences but is merely freed from penalties.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 45
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that he who sees a needy man and passes him by, yet gives his money for indulgences, does not buy papal indulgences but God’s wrath.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 46
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that, unless they have more than they need, they must reserve enough for their family needs and by no means squander it on indulgences.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 47
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that they buying of indulgences is a matter of free choice, not commanded.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 48
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that the pope, in granting indulgences, needs and thus desires their devout prayer more than their money.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 49
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that papal indulgences are useful only if they do not put their trust in them, but very harmful if they lose their fear of God because of them.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 50
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that if the pope knew the exactions of the indulgence preachers, he would rather that the basilica of St. Peter were burned to ashes than built up with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 51
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians are to be taught that the pope would and should wish to give of his own money, even though he had to sell the basilica of St. Peter, to many of those from whom certain hawkers of indulgences cajole money.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 52
author: Martin Luther
snippet: It is vain to trust in salvation by indulgence letters, even though the indulgence commissary, or even the pope, were to offer his soul as security.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 53
author: Martin Luther
snippet: They are the enemies of Christ and the pope who forbid altogether the preaching of the Word of God in some churches in order that indulgences may be preached in others.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 54
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Injury is done to the Word of God when, in the same sermon, an equal or larger amount of time is devoted to indulgences than to the Word.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 55
author: Martin Luther
snippet: It is certainly the pope’s sentiment that if indulgences, which are a very insignificant thing, are celebrated with one bell, one procession, and one ceremony, then the gospel, which is the very greatest thing, should be preached with a hundred bells, a hundred processions, a hun…

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 56
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The true treasures of the church, out of which the pope distributes indulgences, are not sufficiently discussed or known among the people of Christ.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 57
author: Martin Luther
snippet: That indulgences are not temporal treasures is certainly clear, for many indulgence sellers do not distribute them freely but only gather them.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 58
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Nor are they the merits of Christ and the saints, for, even without the pope, the latter always work grace for the inner man, and the cross, death, and hell for the outer man.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 59
author: Martin Luther
snippet: St. Lawrence said that the poor of the church were the treasures of the church, but he spoke according to the usage of the word in his own time.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 60
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Without want of consideration we say that the keys of the church, given by the merits of Christ, are that treasure.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 61
author: Martin Luther
snippet: For it is clear that the pope’s power is of itself sufficient for the remission of penalties and cases reserved by himself.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 62
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The true treasure of the church is the most holy gospel of the glory and grace of God.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 63
author: Martin Luther
snippet: But this treasure is naturally most odious, for it makes the first to be last (Mt. 20:16).

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 64
author: Martin Luther
snippet: On the other hand, the treasure of indulgences is naturally most acceptable, for it makes the last to be first.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 65
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Therefore the treasures of the gospel are nets with which one formerly fished for men of wealth.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 66
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The treasures of indulgences are nets with which one now fishes for the wealth of men.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 67
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The indulgences which the demagogues acclaim as the greatest graces are actually understood to be such only insofar as they promote gain.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 68
author: Martin Luther
snippet: They are nevertheless in truth the most insignificant graces when compared with the grace of God and the piety of the cross.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 69
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Bishops and curates are bound to admit the commissaries of papal indulgences with all reverence.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 70
author: Martin Luther
snippet: But they are much more bound to strain their eyes and ears lest these men preach their own dreams instead of what the pope has commissioned.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 71
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Let him who speaks against the truth concerning papal indulgences be anathema and accursed.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 72
author: Martin Luther
snippet: But let him who guards against the lust and license of the indulgence preachers be blessed.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 73
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Just as the pope justly thunders against those who by any means whatever contrive harm to the sale of indulgences.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 74
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Much more does he intend to thunder against those who use indulgences as a pretext to contrive harm to holy love and truth.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 75
author: Martin Luther
snippet: To consider papal indulgences so great that they could absolve a man even if he had done the impossible and had violated the mother of God is madness.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 76
author: Martin Luther
snippet: We say on the contrary that papal indulgences cannot remove the very least of venial sins as far as guilt is concerned.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 77
author: Martin Luther
snippet: To say that even St. Peter if he were now pope, could not grant greater graces is blasphemy against St. Peter and the pope.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 78
author: Martin Luther
snippet: We say on the contrary that even the present pope, or any pope whatsoever, has greater graces at his disposal, that is, the gospel, spiritual powers, gifts of healing, etc., as it is written. (1 Co 12[:28])

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 79
author: Martin Luther
snippet: To say that the cross emblazoned with the papal coat of arms, and set up by the indulgence preachers is equal in worth to the cross of Christ is blasphemy.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 80
author: Martin Luther
snippet: The bishops, curates, and theologians who permit such talk to be spread among the people will have to answer for this.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 81
author: Martin Luther
snippet: This unbridled preaching of indulgences makes it difficult even for learned men to rescue the reverence which is due the pope from slander or from the shrewd questions of the laity.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 82
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Such as: “Why does not the pope empty purgatory for the sake of holy love and the dire need of the souls that are there if he redeems an infinite number of souls for the sake of miserable money with which to build a church?” The former reason would be most just; the latter is mos…

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 83
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “Why are funeral and anniversary masses for the dead continued and why does he not return or permit the withdrawal of the endowments founded for them, since it is wrong to pray for the redeemed?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 84
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “What is this new piety of God and the pope that for a consideration of money they permit a man who is impious and their enemy to buy out of purgatory the pious soul of a friend of God and do not rather, because of the need of that pious and beloved soul, free it for pure …

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 85
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “Why are the penitential canons, long since abrogated and dead in actual fact and through disuse, now satisfied by the granting of indulgences as though they were still alive and in force?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 86
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “Why does not the pope, whose wealth is today greater than the wealth of the richest Crassus, build this one basilica of St. Peter with his own money rather than with the money of poor believers?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 87
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “What does the pope remit or grant to those who by perfect contrition already have a right to full remission and blessings?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 88
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Again, “What greater blessing could come to the church than if the pope were to bestow these remissions and blessings on every believer a hundred times a day, as he now does but once?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 89
author: Martin Luther
snippet: “Since the pope seeks the salvation of souls rather than money by his indulgences, why does he suspend the indulgences and pardons previously granted when they have equal efficacy?”

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 90
author: Martin Luther
snippet: To repress these very sharp arguments of the laity by force alone, and not to resolve them by giving reasons, is to expose the church and the pope to the ridicule of their enemies and to make Christians unhappy.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 91
author: Martin Luther
snippet: If, therefore, indulgences were preached according to the spirit and intention of the pope, all these doubts would be readily resolved. Indeed, they would not exist.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 92
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Away, then, with all those prophets who say to the people of Christ, “Peace, peace,” and there is no peace! (Jer 6:14)

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 93
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Blessed be all those prophets who say to the people of Christ, “Cross, cross,” and there is no cross!

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 94
author: Martin Luther
snippet: Christians should be exhorted to be diligent in following Christ, their Head, through penalties, death and hell.

title: The 95 Theses — Thesis 95
author: Martin Luther
snippet: And thus be confident of entering into heaven through many tribulations rather than through the false security of peace (Acts 14:22).

title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion — Article 30: Of Both Kinds
snippet: The Cup of the Lord is not to be denied to the Lay-people: for both the parts of the Lord’s Sacrament, by Christ’s ordinance and commandment, ought to be ministered to all Christian men alike.
